name: Stickers by Use
h1: Custom Stickers by Where They Are Used
seoTitle: Stickers by Use: Car, Window, Packaging, Outdoor & Promotional
seoDescription: Pick custom stickers by where they go: cars, storefront windows, product packaging, indoor displays, outdoor equipment and promotional handouts.
tagline: Where a sticker lives decides its material, adhesive and size. Start from the surface and the rest follows.
quickAnswer: Stickers by use groups our products by the surface they go on: vehicles, windows, product packaging, indoor spaces, outdoor equipment and promotional handouts. Each use has a proven material (cast vinyl for cars, clear film for glass, BOPP for wet packaging, paper for indoor and giveaways) and a size range, all cut to any shape from $0.30 per sticker.

sections.h2: Start from the surface, not the sticker
sections.html:
Nearly every sticker that fails in the field was chosen from a product list instead of from the surface it had to live on. A storefront window is cold on one side and sunny on the other. A delivery van gets pressure-washed. A kombucha bottle sweats in a cooler. A trade-show handout lives in a pocket for a day. Each of those is a different adhesive, film and size problem, and the products on this page are grouped so you can start from yours.

  • Vehicles: cast vinyl, laminate, permanent adhesive, 6 to 24 inches.
  • Windows: clear or white vinyl, inside or outside application, 4 to 18 inches.
  • Packaging: BOPP, vinyl or paper by product, rolls or sheets, 1 to 4 inches.
  • Indoor spaces: paper or removable vinyl, 2 to 12 inches.
  • Outdoor equipment: laminated vinyl, 2 to 12 inches.
  • Promotions: paper or vinyl, 2 to 4 inches, die cut or kiss cut.

If your surface is not listed, the step-by-step sticker quote form has a field for it and we pick the material.

Lifespans assume a vertical surface, a clean dry application and a laminate where listed. Horizontal surfaces in full sun lose about a third.

Car and truck stickers face pressure washers, road salt, sun and the flex of a door closing a dozen times a day. Cast vinyl, which is poured rather than rolled, holds its size and shape through all of that; calendered vinyl is acceptable for a short campaign or a flat trailer side. Laminate is not optional on a vehicle. Size by reading distance: a phone number on a door needs letters at least 3 inches tall to be read from the next lane. Fleet work is usually quoted as a set per vehicle with a few spares. The custom car sticker page covers panel-by-panel sizing and the wet application method for large pieces.

A window sticker can go on either side of the glass. Outside-mounted white vinyl reads cleanly against any interior and is the simple choice for hours, logos and promotions. Inside-mounted clear vinyl is reverse-printed so it reads correctly from the street while the glass protects it from weather and vandals; it needs a white underlay behind the design or the colors wash out against the store interior. Removable adhesive suits seasonal promotions; permanent suits anything that stays a year or more. Custom window stickers are priced the same either side, so choose by how long it stays and who will remove it.

Packaging labels are chosen by what the product does to them. Refrigerated drinks, cosmetics and anything used in a kitchen or bathroom need BOPP or vinyl with a permanent adhesive so condensation and oils do not lift them. Dry goods, candles, soap boxes and shipping cartons take paper or kraft, which costs less and prints finer type. Roll supply suits a packing bench; sheets suit hand application in small batches.

  1. Note the container material and whether it is ever cold or wet.
  2. Measure the flat label panel and allow a 0.125-inch safe zone.
  3. Pick BOPP or vinyl for wet, paper for dry.
  4. Choose rolls above a few hundred a week, sheets below.
  5. Apply a 100-piece test run on real containers before the main order.

Format options, roll core sizes and compliance details are on the custom packaging labels page.

Indoor stickers live on walls, doors, shelves, laptops and displays where water and sun are not a problem, so paper or lightly laminated vinyl with removable adhesive does the job and comes off clean when the display changes. Outdoor stickers on equipment, bins, poles and signs need laminated white vinyl with permanent adhesive and simple, high-contrast artwork that still reads after a few seasons of fading. Promotional stickers are the giveaway at a counter or event; the sticker's job is to be kept, so a die cut shape and a gloss finish matter more than longevity. The outdoor stickers for equipment and signage page explains laminate choices, and the indoor and promotional pages cover adhesive and sheet formats.

faqs.q: What sticker material is best for a car door?
faqs.a: Cast vinyl with a gloss or matte laminate and permanent adhesive. Cast film conforms to curves and does not shrink back from the edges, and the laminate handles car washes and sun for three to five years. Calendered vinyl is fine for flat trailer panels or campaigns under a year.

faqs.q: Should window stickers go inside or outside the glass?
faqs.a: Inside if you want weather and vandal protection and can reverse-print on clear vinyl with a white underlay. Outside if the design needs solid white vinyl or the glass is tinted. Both last two to four years; outside-mounted stickers are easier for staff to replace.

faqs.q: Which labels survive a refrigerator or cooler?
faqs.a: BOPP or vinyl with a permanent adhesive, applied to dry containers at room temperature and left 24 hours before chilling. Condensation lifts paper labels within hours. Gloss or matte laminate both work; matte hides scuffs on bottles that get handled often.

faqs.q: Can I use the same sticker indoors and outdoors?
faqs.a: Laminated vinyl with permanent adhesive works in both places. The reverse is not true: paper, kraft and removable-adhesive stickers meant for indoor use will fail outside within weeks. If a design must go both places, order it on the outdoor spec.

faqs.q: How big should a storefront window sticker be?
faqs.a: Big enough to read from the sidewalk or the road, which usually means 6 to 18 inches for a logo and letters at least 2 inches tall for hours or a phone number. Tape a paper print at size on the glass and check it from across the street before ordering.

faqs.q: What is the best sticker for trade show giveaways?
faqs.a: A die cut vinyl sticker, 2.5 to 3.5 inches, gloss finish, with the design that people actually want on a laptop or bottle rather than a plain logo. Vinyl costs a little more than paper but the sticker gets kept and applied instead of binned.

faqs.q: Do outdoor equipment stickers need a laminate?
faqs.a: Yes. Unlaminated vinyl fades and scratches in a season on bins, poles, generators and signs. A gloss laminate roughly doubles outdoor life and makes the sticker wipeable. Keep artwork high-contrast so it stays legible as the colors age.

faqs.q: Can packaging labels be supplied on rolls?
faqs.a: Yes, on standard 3-inch cores with the unwind direction you specify for your dispenser or applicator. Rolls make sense above a few hundred labels a week. Below that, sheets are cheaper and easier to apply by hand.

faqs.q: How do removable stickers for indoor displays come off?
faqs.a: Peel slowly from one corner at a low angle. Removable acrylic adhesive leaves painted walls, glass and laminate clean for up to about two years; after that some residue is possible and a little isopropyl alcohol removes it. Do not use removable adhesive on textured or freshly painted walls.

faqs.q: What size should a promotional sticker be?
faqs.a: Two to four inches. Smaller than 2 inches reads as a label and gets lost; larger than 4 inches does not fit a laptop lid or water bottle, which is where promotional stickers end up. Three inches on the longest side is the safe default.
